content: Otitis media refers to inflammation of the middle ear. The development of antibiotic therapy for otitis media began with the mass production of penicillin in 1940 by Alexander Fleming, Howard Florey, and Ernst Chain. The pathogenesis of otitis media is closely linked to the pathogens responsible for nasopharyngitis, including viral upper respiratory infections and bacterial infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Staphylococcus aureus. Mucus accumulation in the middle ear leads to congestion, which impairs the function of the eustachian tube. This dysfunction alters pressure regulation in the inner ear, resulting in fluid effusion into the tympanic cavity, which contains the pathogens from nasopharyngitis. The inflammatory response to this infection is what causes otitis media. Transmission occurs through respiratory droplets in saliva or mucus, as well as direct contact with contaminated individuals or surfaces. There is evidence of a genetic predisposition to otitis media, with significant heritability. Otitis media can be classified into acute, effusive, and chronic suppurative forms, each presenting with distinct symptoms. Common symptoms across all forms include ear pain and a sensation of fullness in the ear due to fluid buildup in the eustachian tube. These symptoms are often accompanied by ear discharge and partial hearing loss. Acute otitis media is frequently associated with cold symptoms such as cough, nasal discharge, and fever. Chronic otitis media with effusion may present with neurological symptoms in infants and young children, such as irritability, poor coordination, delayed speech development, and reduced attention span. Physical examination using an otoscope often reveals erythema, bulging, cloudiness, and immobility of the tympanic membrane, along with the presence of effusion. Tympanometry can confirm partial hearing loss due to fluid buildup. Imaging studies, such as CT or MRI, may show opacification of the middle ear and mastoid cavity, particularly in cases with complications like mastoiditis or intracranial involvement. The primary treatment for acute otitis media (AOM) is antimicrobial therapy, with high-dose amoxicillin as the first-line antibiotic. If symptoms persist after 48–72 hours, amoxicillin-clavulanate or intramuscular ceftriaxone may be used. Pain management typically involves acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or narcotic analgesics with codeine. Surgical intervention, such as myringotomy with or without tympanostomy tube insertion, is indicated for recurrent or chronic cases unresponsive to medical therapy. This procedure involves creating an incision in the tympanic membrane to drain fluid and relieve pressure. Preventive measures focus on reducing the risk of nasopharyngitis, which includes vaccination against pneumococcal and influenza pathogens, frequent handwashing, and avoiding exposure to respiratory droplets. Minimizing exposure to air pollution and secondhand smoke also helps prevent otitis media. For infants, breastfeeding for at least six months and avoiding pacifiers and daycare enrollment can reduce risk. Prophylactic antibiotics may be considered for at-risk children, and surgical interventions like tympanostomy tube placement may prevent recurrence in chronic or recurrent cases. The prognosis for otitis media is generally favorable, with acute cases often resolving within 14 days and effusive cases within 3–6 months. Chronic suppurative otitis media may require surgical or prolonged antibiotic treatment. Complications, such as tympanic membrane damage or the spread of infection, can increase morbidity and worsen outcomes.
